stories.title: Apollo economist: AI delivers 'zero financial payoff' for most firms
stories.summary: An Apollo Global Management economist argues that most companies adopting AI are seeing no measurable financial return on it, according to a TechCrunch report gaining traction on Hacker News.
stories.more: The claim comes from a TechCrunch article and drew over 200 points and 200 comments on Hacker News, a notably strong response. The item's excerpt doesn't include the economist's methodology or which companies were studied, so the basis for the 'zero payoff' conclusion isn't available here. It adds to a broader, ongoing debate about whether enterprise AI spending is translating into measurable returns.

stories.title: OpenAI may rebrand its data centers as 'AI compute campuses'
stories.summary: TechCrunch reports OpenAI may start calling its data centers 'AI compute campuses,' as data centers face growing public opposition over their resource use.
stories.more: The report frames the possible rename as a response to data centers being unpopular with nearby communities, often over electricity and water use. Renaming infrastructure is a common PR tactic, but the TechCrunch piece suggests it would not change the underlying resource demands of the facilities. No timeline or confirmation of an official rebrand from OpenAI is given in the excerpt.

stories.title: Apriel Voice 27B: an open speech model that reasons and calls tools
stories.summary: Apriel Voice 27B Preview is an open speech-language model that reasons over context and generates tool calls directly from speech, without a separate speech-to-text step.
stories.more: The model is built on a post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint and keeps text and image input alongside speech, so it works across modalities rather than voice alone. Unlike pipelines that transcribe speech before reasoning, Apriel Voice processes speech directly and produces both conversational responses and tool calls within one shared reasoning backbone. The excerpt is cut off before describing benchmark results, so its performance against other open voice assistants isn't given.

stories.title: R2Orch uses recursive self-play to train AI agent orchestrators
stories.summary: A new paradigm, R2Orch, runs an inner self-play loop to improve how AI agents are orchestrated, aiming to fix hand-designed curricula, advantage collapse, and unreliable per-skill evaluation signals in existing methods.
stories.more: Agentic orchestration coordinates multiple AI skills to solve complex tasks, but current training methods rely on hand-designed curricula and can suffer 'advantage collapse' when all rollouts for a task reach the same outcome. Evaluation signals that score each skill with one noisy number add further instability. R2Orch addresses this with Recursive Self-Play Orchestration: an inner loop of self-play that improves the orchestrator itself, inside what the paper calls a skill-internalization loop. The excerpt does not specify which benchmarks or models the method was tested against.

stories.title: CEPO splits coordinator and executor prompts in multi-agent systems
stories.summary: CEPO is a new framework for prompt optimization in multi-agent systems that separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution, using a shared coordinator prompt alongside agent-specific executor prompts.
stories.more: Multi-agent systems need both coordination across agents and specialized execution within each agent, but most prompt-optimization methods couple the two inside agent-specific prompts. Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO) instead separates the two: a shared coordinator prompt handles system-level coordination, while agent-specific executor prompts handle task execution, and the two are updated according to their distinct roles. The excerpt does not include benchmark results, so how much this separation improves over coupled approaches isn't clear yet.

stories.title: Wizard lets agents control and manipulate real-time generated game worlds
stories.summary: Wizard is an agentic framework for real-time, interactive video world models, aiming to let generated virtual environments be manipulated beyond simple, predefined game settings.
stories.more: Video world models can now generate increasingly realistic, interactive environments for player-customizable gameplay, and agentic frameworks have pushed this further by separating game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. The excerpt says existing approaches still support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, and generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters. Wizard is presented as a step toward manipulating 'any world in real time' via agentic control, though the excerpt cuts off before detailing how it works.

stories.title: HiFOR adds hierarchical foresight to vision-language-action robot models
stories.summary: HiFOR is a new vision-language-action model that predicts short-term dynamics and long-term task goals together, aiming to ground a robot's future predictions more tightly in its action policy.
stories.more: Vision-Language-Action models combine visual perception, language understanding and action generation for robotic manipulation, and recent versions add future prediction to better capture environment dynamics and task progression. Existing methods, however, tend to model short-term dynamics and long-term objectives separately, and feed predicted futures into action policies without enough integration. HiFOR proposes hierarchical foresight with action-guided world grounding to unify these levels. The excerpt cuts off before describing results, so its measured gains over prior VLA models aren't given.

stories.title: CaPtain pipeline post-trains code-as-policy robot agents with RL
stories.summary: CaPtain is a training pipeline that applies the standard supervised-fine-tuning-then-RL recipe used for coding and tool-use agents to code-as-policy robot manipulation, where a policy writes and runs code against robot APIs.
stories.more: Language-model agents for coding, web and tool-use tasks are typically trained with supervised fine-tuning to learn an interface, followed by multi-turn reinforcement learning to master it. Code-as-policy casts robot manipulation the same way, with a policy writing code against robot APIs and reading back the results. Existing code-as-policy agents, however, have skipped this training recipe, instead prompting closed frontier models or delegating manipulation to other systems. CaPtain applies the full SFT-then-RL pipeline directly to code-as-policy robot agents, though the excerpt is cut off before giving benchmark results.

stories.title: Paper asks whether AGI needs a System-1 filter before System-2 reasoning
stories.summary: A paper examines whether AGI progress should pair the resource-heavy 'System-2' executive with a lightweight 'System-1' predictor that filters which interactions are worth System-2's cost, instead of relying only on scaling.
stories.more: Most AGI progress has come from scaling System-2, the resource-intensive executive, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. The authors instead study co-designing System-2 with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution. The goal is for System-2 to act only on interactions System-1 judges worth the cost. The excerpt stops before giving quantitative results, so how well this approach performs isn't yet clear.

stories.title: Simon Willison quotes Kyle Kingsbury on LLMs eroding trust in software
stories.summary: Quoting Jepsen's Kyle Kingsbury, Simon Willison highlights concern that LLM use erodes trust in documentation and software, since the old signals of a mature, trustworthy project are now easier to fake.
stories.more: The quote argues that as LLM-generated code and documentation become harder to distinguish from carefully produced work, the signals engineers used to rely on to judge a project's maturity lose their meaning. Kingsbury, known for Jepsen's distributed-systems testing results, asks what maintainers can do to keep software and documentation accurate now that those signals are easier to counterfeit, and how they'd demonstrate that quality to users. The full text of his remarks is cut off in the excerpt, so further specifics aren't available.

stories.title: Simon Willison: delete uv.lock when Python dependency errors confuse you
stories.summary: Simon Willison notes that confusing Python dependency errors, which he started seeing after moving to Python 3.15, are often fixed by simply deleting a stray uv.lock file and letting it regenerate.
stories.more: Willison says most of his projects are libraries that don't ship a uv.lock file, since locking versions is inappropriate for a dependency other projects will use. Commands like 'uv run pytest' can still leave a lock file behind locally, which is gitignored and never committed. When obscure dependency errors appear, his rule of thumb is to delete that stray uv.lock file first before investigating further.
